current_episode.title: Fair banking, good credit and collaboration: Niall Alexander, Fair4All Finance

guest.bio_context: Neil has spent decades working in financial inclusion and community development, tracing his work back to the Tony Blair government's Policy Action Team 14 in 1997 focused on financial exclusion. He was a community worker who helped establish the Westerhales Community Banking Agreement with Bank of Scotland, opening approximately 1,800 bank accounts for unbanked people in an 18-month period. He has subsequently worked as a consultant with multiple CDFIs, for Bank of Scotland, Moneyline, Carnegie UK Trust, and Michael Sheen's End High Cost Credit Alliance before joining Fair4All Finance in August 2021.

It's an extensive conversation drawing on Neil's lengthy experience working with communities and in financial inclusion. Let's hear from Neil now. Yes. I was working for a community development project in Westerhales, a peripheral housing estate in Edinburgh. I'd worked in Craigmiller and then I worked in Westerhales. Yeah. And with some amazing community activists, I helped set up something called the Westerhales Community Banking Agreement, which was an agreement between a bank, in this case, Bank of Scotland, and a community of what was then and is still now, a disadvantaged community of about 9,000 units, mostly social renting and on low incomes. And we had an agreement with the bank, a written agreement, a signed agreement, where we would give them our business, which meant community business. Community organizations of all types agreed that they would bank with the Bank of Scotland And in return, the Bank of Scotland would do things for us like open bank accounts or offer saving and loan schemes, which we ran through the local housing association. And it was a kind of early experiment into much of the stuff that we're still doing, you know, of addressing exclusion. Around that same time, did some work with Michael Sheen's End High Cost Credit Alliance and still have some association with Michael doing some of that work. And then got a job with Fair For All pretty much two years ago, from now, August of 2021. Fascinating plotted career history there, Neil. Well, thanks for that. pending_qa.q: What were the key findings from Fair4All Finance's research on illegal money lending?
pending_qa.r: We Fight Fraud interviewed 287 people with lived experience of relationship-based illegal money lending across Glasgow, Port Talbot, Preston, and South London. The research found that the stereotype of violent illegal lenders was not as prevalent as expected; instead, people viewed illegal lenders pragmatically as their only available alternative after exhausting friends, family, and mainstream finance options. The research also revealed parallel lending, where former employees of defunct home credit companies continue operating informally in housing estates.

pending_qa.q: What role do wraparound services play in responsible community finance lending?
pending_qa.r: Organizations like Fair4All Finance, Moneyline, and Scott Cash embed debt and money advisors, provide benefit calculators, and offer warm referrals to support services. The motivation is to be on the side of the borrower; if credit is not appropriate, people are signposted to debt or money advice, benefit calculators, or grants finders. These not-for-profit organizations have no private shareholders to satisfy and are driven by ensuring the needs of the borrower are aligned with the motivations of the lender.

pending_qa.q: What was the Westerhales Community Banking Agreement and what did it achieve?
pending_qa.r: The Westerhales Community Banking Agreement was a written, signed agreement between Bank of Scotland and the community of Westerhales, a disadvantaged housing estate of about 9,000 units, mostly social renting and on low incomes. In an 18-month period, it opened approximately 1,800 bank accounts for unbanked people using trusted partner status. The agreement also supported saving and loan schemes run through local housing associations and included some micro business lending, pioneering CDFI-related work without initially realizing that's what they were doing.

pending_qa.q: What is the consequence when people lack access to legal forms of credit?
pending_qa.r: If people cannot access forms of credit in a legal way, they will begin to access it in an illegal way. The alternative outcomes include rises in shoplifting, abandoned tenancies, and people unable to support their families, alongside the fundamental issue that credit can never be a solution to incomes, wages, or benefits that do not cover the cost of living.

pending_qa.q: How should policymakers support community finance organizations to meet regulatory requirements while serving underserved populations?
pending_qa.r: While regulation and credit caps are important, there is a case for providing support or subsidy to lenders for marketing, back office operations, IT infrastructure, governance, and wages—recognizing the wraparound care as a social good. The cost of providing that level of attention and support is good for everybody in the long run; the alternative—illegal lending, shoplifting, abandoned tenancies—is not.
